subject: Climate & Environment
title: Lessons from Ancient Oceans
description: A micro-lesson that makes Lessons from Ancient Oceans usable.

hook.text: 55 million years ago, a massive carbon release acidified the ocean. The fossils tell the story.

buildup.text: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum saw CO₂ spike and ocean pH plummet over thousands of years.

discovery.text: Deep-sea sediments from that era show a sharp drop in carbonate shells — they dissolved away.

twist.text: Recovery took over 100,000 years. The ocean doesn't heal quickly from acid damage.

climax.text: Today's CO₂ is rising 10 times faster than during that ancient event.

punchline.text: The ocean remembers the last acid spike. Recovery took 100,000 years.

quiz.question: How long did it take the ocean to recover from ancient acidification?

details.summary: Earth's geological record reveals past episodes of rapid ocean acidification and warming, such as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum 56 million years ago. Marine extinctions during these events offer sobering parallels to the changes occurring in today's oceans.
details.whyItMatters: Studying ancient ocean crises reveals how marine ecosystems respond to rapid chemical change and helps scientists predict what current acidification trends could mean for biodiversity.
takeaways: The PETM caused massive ocean acidification 56 million years ago
Ancient events triggered widespread marine extinctions
Today's rate of CO2 increase is faster than during the PETM

faq.question: What happened during the PETM?
faq.answer: A massive release of carbon over a few thousand years raised global temperatures by about 5 degrees C and acidified the oceans. Deep-sea foraminifera suffered widespread extinction, and recovery took roughly 200,000 years.

faq.question: How does today's carbon release compare to the PETM?
faq.answer: Humans are releasing carbon dioxide at least ten times faster than during the PETM. This unprecedented rate gives marine organisms far less time to adapt, raising the risk of more severe ecosystem disruption than the geological record shows.
